learn.hook: A seat in a cinema is 'Row F, Seat 12' — not 'Seat F, Row 12'. Order matters, and that is the heart of an ordered pair.
points: Relations and functions are built by pairing elements of one set with elements of another.
An ordered pair (a, b) has a first and a second element. (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d. So (2, 3) ≠ (3, 2).
Cartesian product: A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}. If A or B is ∅, then A × B = ∅.
If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A × B) = pq.
In general A × B ≠ B × A; they are equal only when A = B (or one of them is empty).

steps: Equate first elements: x/3 + 1 = 5/3, so x/3 = 2/3 and x = 2.
Equate second elements: y − 2/3 = 1/3, so y = 1.

learn.reallife: A pizza menu with 4 bases and 3 toppings offers 4 × 3 = 12 pizza combinations — every (base, topping) ordered pair of a Cartesian product.

games.title: Ordered pair rules
items: Order matters: first elements 2 and 5 differ.
If A = {1, 2} and B = {x}, then A × B = {(1, x), (2, x)}.
Pair each element of A with x.
A × ∅ = ∅ for every set A.
There is no second element to pair with.
If n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 4, then n(A × B) = 7.
A × B = B × A for all non-empty sets A and B.
(a, b) = (c, d) means a = c and b = d.
That is the definition of equal ordered pairs.

quiz.q: If (x + 1, y − 2) = (3, 1), what is x + y?
quiz.explain: x + 1 = 3 gives x = 2; y − 2 = 1 gives y = 3. So x + y = 5.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding when solving y − 2 = 1

quiz.q: A = {1, 2} and B = {3, 4}. Which is A × B?
quiz.explain: Pair every element of A (first) with every element of B (second).
steps: A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}, with first entry from A
quiz.mistake: Puts B's elements first, or pairs only matching positions

quiz.q: If n(A) = 4 and n(B) = 6, then n(A × B) is:
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers of elements instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Which is true if A = {a} and B = ∅?
quiz.explain: There is no element of B to pair with a, so no ordered pair can be formed.
steps: A × B needs pairs (a, b) with b ∈ B
B = ∅ has no element to pair with a
So no ordered pair can be formed
quiz.mistake: Treats ∅ as an element that can be paired

quiz.q: If A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}, which pair is in B × A but NOT in A × B?
quiz.explain: (3, 1) has first element from B and second from A; 3 ∉ A, so it cannot be in A × B. (2, 2) is in both.
steps: In B × A the first entry is from B = {2, 3}, the second from A = {1, 2}
In A × B the first entry must be in A, but 3 ∉ A
So (3, 1) is in B × A but not in A × B
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the first element of a pair in A × B must come from A

quiz.explain: 2a − 1 = 5 gives a = 3; b + 1 = 3 gives b = 2.
steps: Equal ordered pairs: first = first, second = second
quiz.mistake: Swaps the values or solves b + 1 = 3 as b = 4

quiz.q: For non-empty sets A and B, A × B = B × A holds exactly when:
quiz.explain: If A ≠ B, some element lies in one set only, giving a pair in one product but not the other.
steps: Suppose A ≠ B, say a ∈ A but a ∉ B
Take any b ∈ B: (a, b) ∈ A × B, but (a, b) ∉ B × A, since its first entry is not in B
So the products can be equal only when the sets are equal
A × B = B × A exactly when A = B
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal sizes are enough

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5}, then A × B has 6 elements.
Reason (R): n(A × B) = n(A) + n(B).
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A × B has 3 × 2 = 6 pairs, so A is true. But the rule is a product, n(A) · n(B), not a sum; R is false.
steps: n(A) = 3, n(B) = 2, so n(A × B) = 3 × 2 = 6 → A is true
R says n(A) + n(B) = 3 + 2 = 5, which is not 6
The correct rule is a product, so R is false
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Adds sizes instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu thinks (Row 3, Seat 5) is the same as (Row 5, Seat 3). Explain ordered pairs and how A × B is formed.
teach.praise: So order matters and A × B pairs everyone with everyone. I'll sit in the right seat now!
teach.nudge: Does (3, 5) equal (5, 3)? And how many pairs does A × B have?

revise.summary: An ordered pair (a, b) has a fixed first and second element, and A × B is the set of all pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A × B) = pq.
focus: Write A × B by pairing every element of A (first) with every element of B (second)
Use equality of ordered pairs to find unknowns
Count n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B)
Know when A × B = B × A and that A × ∅ = ∅
remember: (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d
A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}
n(A × B) = pq when n(A) = p and n(B) = q
traps: (2, 3) ≠ (3, 2): order matters in an ordered pair
Don't add n(A) and n(B): n(A × B) is their product

topics.title: Triplets and reading back the sets

learn.hook: A drone over Bengaluru needs three numbers — latitude-style x, y and height z. That is an ordered triplet from R × R × R.
points: A × A × A = {(a, b, c) : a, b, c ∈ A}; each (a, b, c) is an ordered triplet.
R × R is the coordinate plane (all points (x, y)); R × R × R is three-dimensional space.
If n(A) = k, then n(A × A) = k² and n(A × A × A) = k³.
To recover A and B from A × B: collect all first elements to get A and all second elements to get B.
If only some elements of A × B are given, A must contain all their first elements and B all their second elements.

example.q: A × B = {(p, q), (p, r), (m, q), (m, r)}. Find A and B.
steps: First elements: p, m, so A = {p, m}.
Second elements: q, r, so B = {q, r}.

learn.reallife: ISRO tracks a satellite with three coordinates at each instant — every position is an ordered triplet in R × R × R.

games.title: Match the product with its count

quiz.q: If A = {−1, 1}, how many elements does A × A × A have?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 2 by 3 instead of raising 2 to the power 3

quiz.q: Which ordered triplet is in A × A × A for A = {0, 1}?
quiz.explain: Each entry must come from {0, 1}. (1, 0, 1) qualifies; 2 and −1 are not in A, and (0, 1) is a pair.
steps: Every entry of a triplet in A × A × A must come from A = {0, 1}
(−1, 0, 1) has −1 and (1, 2, 0) has 2, which are not in A
(0, 1) is a pair, not a triplet
quiz.mistake: Ignores that every coordinate must lie in A

quiz.q: If A × A has 9 elements and two of them are (−1, 0) and (0, 1), find A.
quiz.explain: n(A)² = 9 so n(A) = 3. The given pairs show −1, 0 and 1 are in A, so A = {−1, 0, 1}.
steps: From (−1, 0) and (0, 1): −1, 0 and 1 are all in A
That is 3 elements already, so there are no others
quiz.mistake: Stops at the elements seen without using n(A) = 3

quiz.q: A × B = {(a, x), (a, y), (b, x), (b, y), (c, x), (c, y)}. What is n(A)?
quiz.explain: The first elements are a, b, c, so A = {a, b, c} and n(A) = 3.
steps: A = set of all first elements of A × B
First elements: a, a, b, b, c, c → {a, b, c}
quiz.mistake: Counts the pairs instead of the distinct first elements

quiz.q: The set R × R can be identified with:
options: all points of the coordinate plane
all points on a number line
quiz.explain: Each (x, y) with real x and y is a point of the plane.
steps: R × R = {(x, y) : x, y ∈ R}
Each pair of real coordinates (x, y) gives one point of the plane
A number line uses one coordinate; space needs three
R × R = all points of the coordinate plane
Answer: all points of the coordinate plane
quiz.mistake: Confuses R × R with R or with R × R × R

quiz.q: If n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 2, then n((A × B) × B) is:
quiz.explain: n(A × B) = 6, and then × B gives 6 × 2 = 12.
steps: n((A × B) × B) = n(A × B) × n(B)
quiz.mistake: Uses n(A) twice instead of n(B)

quiz.q: A = {1, 2} and B = {3, 4}. Which statement is true?
quiz.explain: In A × B the first entry is from A and the second from B; in B × A it is the other way round.
steps: In A × B the first entry is from A = {1, 2}, the second from B = {3, 4}
True statement: (1, 4) ∈ A × B and (4, 1) ∈ B × A
Answer: (1, 4) ∈ A × B and (4, 1) ∈ B × A
quiz.mistake: Forgets which set supplies the first entry

quiz.q: If P = {a, b} and Q = {b, c}, then n(P × Q) − n(P ∩ Q) =
quiz.mistake: Counts P × Q as having 3 elements because b is common

teach.ask: Gappu's friend sent only the list A × B. Explain to Gappu how to find A and B from it, and what A × A × A means.
teach.praise: First entries make A, second entries make B. Detective work done!
teach.nudge: Which entries of the pairs tell you the set A?

revise.summary: An ordered triplet (a, b, c) is an element of A × A × A. If n(A) = k then n(A × A) = k² and n(A × A × A) = k³; from A × B, the first elements give A and the second elements give B.
focus: Count elements of A × A and A × A × A
Recover A and B from a listed A × B
Find A from part of A × A and its size
Know that R × R is the plane and R × R × R is space
remember: n(A × A) = k² and n(A × A × A) = k³ when n(A) = k
A = set of first elements of A × B; B = set of second elements
R × R = coordinate plane; R × R × R = three-dimensional space
traps: Don't mix up (1, 4) ∈ A × B with (4, 1): the first entry must come from the first set
Don't count repeated first elements twice when finding n(A)

learn.hook: 'Is a student of' links names to schools; 'is the capital of' links cities to states. Every such link is a relation — a chosen subset of a Cartesian product.
points: A relation R from A to B is any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R, b is the image of a and a is a pre-image of b.
Domain = set of first elements of R; codomain = B; range = set of second elements (images). Range ⊆ codomain.
A relation can be shown in roster form, in set-builder form, or by an arrow diagram.
If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A × B) = pq and the number of relations from A to B is 2^(pq).
∅ and A × B themselves are also relations from A to B.

example.q: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. R = {(x, y) : y = x + 1} on A. Write R in roster form; find its domain and range.

learn.reallife: An IPL auction sheet relating players to franchises is a relation: domain = players sold, range = teams that bought someone.

games.title: How many relations from A to B?

quiz.q: If n(A) = 2 and n(B) = 3, how many relations are there from A to B?
quiz.explain: n(A × B) = 6, and every subset of A × B is a relation, so there are 2⁶ = 64.
quiz.mistake: Gives n(A × B) = 6 instead of 2^6

quiz.q: R = {(x, x²) : x is a prime number less than 8}. What is the range of R?
quiz.explain: Primes below 8 are 2, 3, 5, 7; their squares are 4, 9, 25, 49.
steps: 1 is not prime, so 1 is not an image
quiz.mistake: Gives the domain, or treats 1 as prime

quiz.explain: The range has only the images actually used. 15 is in the codomain but no element maps to it.
steps: 15 ∈ B but nothing maps to it, so range ≠ codomain
quiz.mistake: Thinks range and codomain are always the same

quiz.q: Which set-builder form describes R = {(1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), (4, 16)} on N?
options: {(x, y) : y = x², x ∈ N, x ≤ 4}
quiz.explain: Each second element is the square of the first, for x = 1 to 4.
steps: Second element = square of the first: 1², 2², 3², 4²
Answer: {(x, y) : y = x², x ∈ N, x ≤ 4}
quiz.mistake: Reads the rule backwards (x = y²)

quiz.q: A relation R on Z is {(a, b) : a − b is divisible by 5}. Which pair is in R?
quiz.explain: 12 − 2 = 10, which is divisible by 5. The others give 4, 6 and 4.
steps: Rule: a − b must be divisible by 5
quiz.mistake: Checks a + b instead of a − b

quiz.q: R = {(x, y) : x + 2y = 8, x, y ∈ N}. What is the domain of R?
quiz.explain: y = (8 − x)/2 must be natural: x = 2 → y = 3, x = 4 → 2, x = 6 → 1. x = 8 gives y = 0, not natural.
steps: x + 2y = 8 → y = (8 − x)/2, and y must be natural
Odd x give non-whole y; x = 8 gives y = 0, which is not natural
quiz.mistake: Allows y = 0 or lists the range

quiz.q: An arrow diagram from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b} has arrows 1 → a, 2 → a, 3 → b. In roster form the relation is:
quiz.explain: Each arrow from x to y gives the ordered pair (x, y).
steps: Each arrow x → y gives the ordered pair (x, y)
1 → a gives (1, a); 2 → a gives (2, a); 3 → b gives (3, b)
quiz.mistake: Writes the pairs backwards

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B.
Reason (R): Every subset of A × B is a function from A to B.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is the definition of a relation. R is false: a subset such as {(1, a), (1, b)} gives 1 two images, so it is not a function.
steps: A is the definition of a relation, so A is true
R: the subset {(1, a), (1, b)} gives 1 two images
That is not a function, so R is false
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks every relation is automatically a function

teach.ask: Gappu drew arrows from names to cities and wants the right words. Explain relation, domain, codomain and range.
teach.praise: Domain sends, range receives, codomain is the whole waiting room. Perfect!
teach.nudge: What is the difference between the range and the codomain?

revise.summary: A relation R from A to B is any subset of A × B. Its domain is the set of first elements, its range the set of images, and the codomain is B; there are 2^(pq) relations from A to B.
focus: Write a relation in roster form from a rule or an arrow diagram
Find domain, range and codomain, knowing range ⊆ codomain
Check whether a given pair satisfies a relation's rule
Count relations: 2^(pq) when n(A) = p, n(B) = q
remember: Relation from A to B: any subset of A × B
Domain = first elements; range = second elements (images); codomain = B
Number of relations from A to B = 2^(pq)
traps: The range is not always the whole codomain: unused elements of B are not in the range
Not every relation is a function

topics.title: What makes a relation a function

learn.hook: A vending machine is a function: press one button and you get exactly one snack. If a button gave you two different snacks at random, it wouldn't be a function!
points: A function f from A to B is a relation in which EVERY element of A has EXACTLY ONE image in B. We write f : A → B.
Test: no element of the domain is left out, and no element appears as a first element in two different pairs.
Two elements of A may share the same image — that is still a function.
A real-valued function has codomain R (or a subset of R). If its domain is also a subset of R, it is a real function.
f(a) is the image of a: substitute a in the rule. E.g. f(x) = x² + 1 gives f(−2) = 5.

example.q: Is R = {(2, 1), (5, 1), (8, 1), (11, 1), (14, 1)} a function? Find its domain and range.
steps: All map to 1 — sharing an image is allowed.

learn.reallife: Every Aadhaar number points to exactly one person's record — a function from Aadhaar numbers to residents.

games.title: Function or not?
items: Student → roll number in a class
Number → its square roots (both signs)

quiz.q: Which relation from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b, c} is a function?
quiz.explain: Each of 1, 2, 3 has exactly one image. The others give 1 or 2 two images, or leave 3 with none.
steps: Function test: each of 1, 2, 3 must have exactly one image
{(2, a), (3, b), (2, c)}: 2 has two images and 1 none; {(1, b), (2, c)}: 3 has none
{(1, a), (2, a), (3, c)}: one image each → function
quiz.mistake: Thinks two inputs sharing an image breaks the rule

quiz.q: If f(x) = x² − 3x + 2, then f(−1) is:
quiz.mistake: Takes (−1)² as −1, or −3(−1) as −3

quiz.q: f(x) = 2x + 3. For which x is f(x) = 11?
quiz.explain: 2x + 3 = 11 gives 2x = 8, so x = 4.
quiz.mistake: Substitutes 11 into f instead of solving f(x) = 11

quiz.q: Why is {(x, y) : x = y², x ∈ {1, 4}} NOT a function of x?
options: x = 4 is paired with both y = 2 and y = −2
The domain has only two elements
quiz.explain: One input with two different outputs violates 'exactly one image'.
steps: For x = 4: 4 = y² gives y = 2 or y = −2
So 4 is paired with two different y values
A function needs exactly one image for each input
Not a function: x = 4 is paired with both y = 2 and y = −2
Answer: x = 4 is paired with both y = 2 and y = −2
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative outputs are not allowed in a function

quiz.q: The relation f = {(x, x²) : x ∈ R} is:
options: not a function, because 2 and −2 have the same image
quiz.explain: Every real x has exactly one square. Two inputs sharing an output is allowed.
steps: Each real x has exactly one square x²
2 and −2 both give 4, but sharing an image is allowed
x² is defined for every real x, so the domain is R
f is a function with domain R
Answer: a function with domain R
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'many-to-one' with 'not a function'

quiz.q: For a real function f(x) = 1/(x − 2), the value f(2.5) is:
quiz.mistake: Divides 2.5 by 2 or forgets the reciprocal

quiz.q: Which statement about a function f : A → B is correct?
options: Every element of A must have exactly one image
Every element of B must have a pre-image
A and B must have the same number of elements
Two elements of A cannot have the same image
quiz.explain: Only the domain condition is required. B may have unused elements and images may repeat.
steps: Function rule: every element of A has exactly one image
B may have elements with no pre-image, and images may repeat
A and B need not have the same size
Answer: Every element of A must have exactly one image
quiz.mistake: Puts the 'exactly one' condition on B instead of A

quiz.q: f(x) = x² for x ∈ R. What is f(3) − f(−3)?
quiz.explain: f(3) = 9 and f(−3) = 9, so the difference is 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks f(−3) = −9

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a function can't send two inputs to the same output. Explain exactly when a relation is a function.
teach.praise: One input, one output — but sharing outputs is fine. Got it!
teach.nudge: Is it a problem if two inputs have the same image? What is the real rule?

revise.summary: A function f : A → B is a relation in which every element of A has exactly one image in B. Different inputs may share an image, and f(a) is found by substituting a in the rule.
focus: Test a relation: every domain element used, and no element with two images
Find f(a) by substitution and solve f(x) = k
Recognise real-valued and real functions
remember: Function: every element of A has exactly one image in B
Two elements of A may share the same image; it is still a function
f(a) is the image of a: substitute a in the rule
traps: A relation where one input has two outputs (like x = y²) is not a function
B may have elements with no pre-image; that does not stop f being a function

topics.title: Domain and range of real functions

learn.hook: A calculator flashes ERROR for √(−4) or 1/0. Finding the domain is just listing every input that does NOT make the calculator complain.
points: Unless stated, the domain of a real function is the largest subset of R for which the formula gives a real value.
Square roots: the expression under √ must be ≥ 0. Fractions: the denominator must not be 0.
Range: the set of all outputs. Work it out from the formula, e.g. x² ≥ 0 so x² + 2 ≥ 2.
From a graph: the domain is the spread of the curve along the x-axis, and the range is its spread along the y-axis.
Examples: √(x − 3) has domain [3, ∞); √(9 − x²) has domain [−3, 3] and range [0, 3].

steps: It is zero at x = 2 and x = 6.
All other real numbers are allowed.

learn.reallife: A cab app's function 'fare from distance' has domain 'distances ≥ 0' and range 'fares from the base fare upwards' — negative kilometres make no sense.

games.title: Match the function with its domain
Match the function with its range

quiz.q: The domain of f(x) = √(x − 5) is:
quiz.explain: Need x − 5 ≥ 0, i.e. x ≥ 5. Zero under the root is allowed, so 5 is included.
steps: Need x − 5 ≥ 0 under the square root
x = 5 gives √0 = 0, which is allowed, so 5 is included
quiz.mistake: Excludes 5, forgetting √0 = 0 is real

quiz.q: The domain of f(x) = 1/(x² − 9) is:
quiz.explain: x² − 9 = 0 at x = ±3, so both must be removed.
quiz.mistake: Removes only the positive root

quiz.q: The range of f(x) = √(9 − x²) is:
quiz.explain: 9 − x² runs from 0 to 9 on the domain [−3, 3], so its square root runs from 0 to 3.
steps: On this domain 9 − x² takes values from 0 (x = ±3) to 9 (x = 0)
√ of values from 0 to 9 runs from 0 to 3
quiz.mistake: Gives the domain instead of the range

quiz.q: The range of f(x) = x² + 3, x ∈ R, is:
quiz.explain: x² ≥ 0 with minimum 0 at x = 0, so f(x) ≥ 3 and 3 is attained.
steps: x² ≥ 0 for every real x, with x² = 0 at x = 0
So x² + 3 ≥ 3, and f(0) = 3 is attained
x² can be as large as we like
quiz.mistake: Ignores the +3 or excludes the minimum value

quiz.q: The domain of f(x) = 1/√(x + 2) is:
quiz.explain: Need x + 2 > 0: strictly positive, because √0 = 0 would make the denominator zero.
steps: Need x + 2 ≥ 0 for the root, and √(x + 2) ≠ 0 for the denominator
quiz.mistake: Uses ≥ even though the root is in the denominator

quiz.q: A graph is a straight segment from (−2, 1) to (4, 7), end points included. Its range is:
quiz.explain: The y-values run from 1 to 7. The x-values (−2 to 4) give the domain.
steps: Range = spread of the graph along the y-axis
End points included, so use square brackets
quiz.mistake: Reads the domain off the x-axis and calls it the range

quiz.q: The range of f(x) = 1 − |x − 2| is:
quiz.explain: |x − 2| ≥ 0, so 1 − |x − 2| ≤ 1, with 1 reached at x = 2. It can be as negative as we like.
steps: At x = 2: f(2) = 1 − 0 = 1, so 1 is attained
As x moves away from 2, |x − 2| grows without limit, so f(x) can be any value below 1
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign flips the inequality

quiz.q: How many integers are in the domain of f(x) = √(4 − x²)?
quiz.explain: Domain is [−2, 2], containing −2, −1, 0, 1, 2: five integers.
quiz.mistake: Excludes the end points ±2

teach.ask: Gappu's calculator keeps saying ERROR. Explain how to find the domain and range of a real function like √(x − 3) or 1/(x − 2).
teach.praise: No negatives under the root, no zero downstairs. My calculator and I are friends again!
teach.nudge: What two things can make a formula give no real value?

revise.summary: The domain of a real function is the largest set of real x for which the formula gives a real value: no negative under √ and no zero denominator. The range is the set of all outputs.
focus: Find domains of square-root and fraction functions
Find ranges using facts like x² ≥ 0 and |x| ≥ 0
Read domain and range from a graph
remember: Under √ the expression must be ≥ 0; a denominator must not be 0
√(x − 3) has domain [3, ∞); √(9 − x²) has domain [−3, 3] and range [0, 3]
Domain: spread of the graph along the x-axis; range: spread along the y-axis
traps: Don't forget both roots: x² − 9 = 0 at x = 3 and x = −3

topics.title: Identity, constant, polynomial and rational functions

learn.hook: A photocopier set to 100% is the identity function; a flat-fee parking lot is a constant function. Graphs make these personalities visible.
points: Identity function f(x) = x on R: domain and range R; graph is the line y = x through the origin at 45°.
Constant function f(x) = c: domain R, range {c}; graph is a horizontal line y = c.
Polynomial function: f(x) = a₀ + a₁x + … + aₙxⁿ with real coefficients and n a non-negative integer. y = x² is a U-shaped parabola (range [0, ∞)); y = x³ rises through the origin (range R).
Rational function: f(x)/g(x) of two polynomials, defined where g(x) ≠ 0.
y = 1/x: domain and range R − {0}; the graph has two branches, in the first and third quadrants, never touching the axes.

example.q: Is f(x) = (x² + 1)/(x − 1) a polynomial function, a rational function or neither? State its domain.
steps: Denominator x − 1 is zero at x = 1, which must be excluded.
It is not a polynomial because it does not simplify to one.

learn.reallife: Boyle's law PV = constant gives P = k/V, the shape of y = 1/x — which is why pressure in a syringe shoots up as you squeeze the volume small.

games.title: Classify the function
items: x³ − 2x + 7
5 (a constant)
x² − 4x

games.title: Match the graph description
pairs: Rises through origin, negative for x < 0
Two branches in quadrants I and III

quiz.q: The range of the constant function f(x) = −4, x ∈ R, is:
quiz.explain: Every input gives −4, so the only output is −4.
steps: The range is the set of outputs
quiz.mistake: Gives the domain R as the range

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a polynomial function?
quiz.explain: 1/x = x⁻¹ has a negative power, so x² + 1/x is not a polynomial. A constant is a polynomial of degree 0.
steps: Polynomial: only non-negative integer powers of x
f(x) = x² + 1/x is NOT a polynomial
quiz.mistake: Thinks a constant cannot be a polynomial

quiz.q: The domain of the rational function f(x) = (x + 2)/(x² − 5x + 6) is:
quiz.explain: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 at x = 2, 3. The numerator's zero −2 does not matter.
steps: Remove zeros of the denominator: x² − 5x + 6 = 0
The numerator's zero (−2) does not affect the domain
quiz.mistake: Removes the zero of the numerator instead

quiz.q: The graph of y = 1/x lies in which quadrants?
quiz.explain: x > 0 gives y > 0 (quadrant I); x < 0 gives y < 0 (quadrant III).
steps: y = 1/x has the same sign as x
quiz.mistake: Confuses 1/x with −1/x

quiz.q: For f(x) = x³, what is f(−2) + f(2)?
quiz.explain: f(−2) = −8 and f(2) = 8; they cancel.
quiz.mistake: Thinks (−2)³ = 8

quiz.q: Which statement about the identity function f(x) = x on R is correct?
options: It is not defined at x = 0
Its graph is parallel to the x-axis
Its range is R and its graph passes through the origin
quiz.explain: f maps each x to itself, so range = R and f(0) = 0.
steps: f(x) = x sends each x to itself
So every real number is an output: range = R
f(0) = 0, so the graph y = x passes through the origin
Answer: Its range is R and its graph passes through the origin
quiz.mistake: Confuses identity function with constant function 1

quiz.q: The range of f(x) = x², x ∈ R, is:
quiz.explain: Squares are never negative and 0 = 0² is attained.
steps: Every non-negative number is a square (e.g. 9 = 3²)
quiz.mistake: Excludes 0 or allows negative squares

quiz.q: For f(x) = 1/x, what is f(1/4) − f(4)?
quiz.explain: f(1/4) = 4 and f(4) = 1/4, so the difference is 4 − 1/4 = 15/4.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order or adds

teach.ask: Gappu must sketch y = x, y = 3, y = x², y = x³ and y = 1/x for a test. Explain what each graph looks like and its range.
teach.praise: Line, flat line, U, S-curve and two branches. My sketchbook is ready!
teach.nudge: Which of these graphs never touches either axis?

revise.summary: Common real functions: identity f(x) = x (range R), constant f(x) = c (range {c}), polynomials such as x² and x³, rational functions p(x)/q(x) defined where q(x) ≠ 0, and 1/x with domain and range R − {0}.
focus: Identify polynomial and rational functions
Find the domain of a rational function by removing zeros of the denominator
Know the graphs and ranges of x, c, x², x³ and 1/x
Evaluate these functions at given points
remember: Identity f(x) = x: domain and range R; constant f(x) = c: range {c}
Polynomial: a₀ + a₁x + … + aₙxⁿ, n a non-negative integer; x² has range [0, ∞), x³ has range R
Rational function f(x)/g(x) is defined where g(x) ≠ 0
y = 1/x: domain and range R − {0}; graph in quadrants I and III
traps: 1/x has a negative power (x⁻¹), so x² + 1/x is not a polynomial
Only zeros of the denominator are removed from the domain, not zeros of the numerator

topics.title: Modulus, signum and greatest integer functions

learn.hook: Distance never goes negative, a cricket umpire's signal is 'out, not out or wait', and a parking lot charges for every started hour. Meet |x|, signum and [x].
points: Modulus: |x| = x if x ≥ 0 and −x if x < 0. Domain R, range [0, ∞); graph is a V with vertex at the origin.
Signum: f(x) = 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0 (equal to |x|/x for x ≠ 0). Domain R, range {−1, 0, 1}.
Greatest integer function [x]: the greatest integer less than or equal to x. [2.7] = 2, [−2.7] = −3, [5] = 5.
[x] has domain R and range Z; its graph is a staircase with a filled dot at the left end of each step and a hollow dot at the right.
For −1 ≤ x < 0, [x] = −1; for 0 ≤ x < 1, [x] = 0; and so on.
learn.reallife: Indian Railways' fare table rounds a journey of 251–300 km into one slab — that is a step function just like [x].

games.title: Special function facts
items: The range of |x| is [0, ∞).
|x| ≥ 0 and every non-negative value is attained.
−1 is greater than −1.5; the greatest integer ≤ −1.5 is −2.
The range of the signum function is {−1, 0, 1}.
Those are its only three outputs.
The graph of |x| is a V shape with vertex at (0, 0).
Two rays y = x and y = −x meeting at the origin.
[x] = x for every integer x.
An integer is the greatest integer not exceeding itself.
The domain of the greatest integer function is Z.
Its domain is R; its range is Z.

quiz.q: What is [−4.2]?
quiz.explain: −5 ≤ −4.2 < −4, so the greatest integer not exceeding −4.2 is −5.
steps: −4 is bigger than −4.2, so it is not allowed
quiz.mistake: Simply drops the decimal part, giving −4

quiz.q: The range of the signum function is:
quiz.explain: The function takes only the values −1 (x < 0), 0 (x = 0) and 1 (x > 0).
steps: Signum takes the value 1 for x > 0, 0 for x = 0 and −1 for x < 0
No other value is ever produced
So the range is the set of these three numbers
quiz.mistake: Forgets the value 0 at x = 0

quiz.q: For x < 0, |x| equals:
quiz.explain: If x is negative, −x is positive, and that is the distance from 0.
steps: Definition: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, and −x for x < 0
For negative x, −x is positive, e.g. x = −5 gives −x = 5
That is the distance of x from 0
quiz.mistake: Thinks |x| = x always
Takes [−2.5] = −2 and gets 0

quiz.q: Which value of x gives [x] = 3?
quiz.explain: 3 ≤ x < 4 gives [x] = 3. 3.99 lies in this interval; 4 gives 4 and 2.99 gives 2.
quiz.mistake: Includes the right end point 4

quiz.q: f(x) = |x|/x for x ≠ 0. What is f(−3)?
quiz.explain: |−3|/(−3) = 3/(−3) = −1. This is the signum function for x ≠ 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the denominator is negative

quiz.q: Which statement about the graph of y = [x] is true?
options: It is a straight line through the origin
On [1, 2) it is the horizontal segment y = 1 with a filled dot at x = 1 and a hollow dot at x = 2
quiz.explain: [x] is constant on each interval [n, n + 1), so the graph is a staircase.
steps: On [1, 2): [x] = 1, a horizontal segment at y = 1
x = 1 is included (filled dot); at x = 2 the value jumps to 2 (hollow dot)
Horizontal segment y = 1 on [1, 2), filled dot at x = 1, hollow dot at x = 2
Answer: On [1, 2) it is the horizontal segment y = 1 with a filled dot at x = 1 and a hollow dot at x = 2
quiz.mistake: Confuses [x] with x or |x|

quiz.q: How many integer values of x satisfy |x| < 3?
quiz.mistake: Includes ±3

teach.ask: Gappu thinks [−2.5] = −2 and that |x| is always just x. Teach Gappu the modulus, signum and greatest integer functions.
teach.praise: So [−2.5] is −3 — step DOWN, not towards zero. Mind officially blown!
teach.nudge: For a negative number like −2.5, is the greatest integer below it −2 or −3?

revise.summary: The modulus |x| gives the distance from 0, the signum function gives 1, 0 or −1 by the sign of x, and the greatest integer function [x] gives the greatest integer ≤ x, with range Z.
focus: Evaluate |x|, signum x and [x], especially for negative numbers
State domain and range: |x| → [0, ∞), signum → {−1, 0, 1}, [x] → Z
Describe the graphs: V shape for |x|, staircase for [x]
Solve simple conditions like [x] = 3 or |x| < 3
remember: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and −x if x < 0
Signum: 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0; equals |x|/x for x ≠ 0
[x] = n for n ≤ x < n + 1
traps: [−4.2] is −5, not −4: go down to the integer on the left
The signum range is {−1, 0, 1}, not the interval [−1, 1]

learn.hook: A startup's profit is revenue minus cost: P(x) = R(x) − C(x). Adding, subtracting and dividing functions is everyday business maths.
points: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) and (f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x), on the common domain D_f ∩ D_g.
(fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g; (αf)(x) = α f(x) for a real constant α.
(f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g, excluding points where g(x) = 0.
Piecewise functions use different rules on different intervals; check that overlapping pieces agree.
Difference quotient: [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. For f(x) = x², [f(1.1) − f(1)]/(1.1 − 1) = 0.21/0.1 = 2.1.

example.q: f(x) = √x and g(x) = x are defined on non-negative reals. Find (f + g)(x), (fg)(x) and (f/g)(x) with domains.
steps: f/g = √x/x = 1/√x, but g(0) = 0, so exclude x = 0.

learn.reallife: A Mumbai dabbawala's daily earning E(x) = 20x − 150 (₹20 per tiffin, ₹150 fixed cost) is a linear function found from two data points.

games.title: Find the domain of f/g for f(x) = √(x − 1), g(x) = x − 4
items: Domain of f: x − 1 ≥ 0, so [1, ∞)
g is defined for all real x, so the common domain is [1, ∞)
Find where g(x) = 0: x = 4
Remove it: domain of f/g = [1, ∞) − {4}

games.title: Compute at x = 2 for f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1

quiz.q: If f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1, then (f − g)(3) is:
quiz.mistake: Computes g − f

quiz.q: For f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x − 1, (f/g)(x) is defined for:
quiz.explain: f/g needs g(x) ≠ 0, i.e. x ≠ 1.
steps: Both f and g are defined for all real x
quiz.mistake: Excludes the zero of f instead of g

quiz.q: f(x) = 2x, g(x) = x² − 1. Find (fg)(−2).
quiz.mistake: Takes (−2)² − 1 as −5

quiz.explain: f(1.1) = 1.21, so the numerator is 0.21; dividing by 0.1 gives 2.1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 0.1

quiz.q: A linear function f(x) = ax + b has f(0) = −1 and f(2) = 3. What is a?
quiz.mistake: Uses the slope from the wrong pair of values

quiz.q: f(x) = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 and 3x for 3 ≤ x ≤ 10. What is f(3)?
quiz.explain: Both pieces give 9 at x = 3 (3² = 9 and 3 × 3 = 9), so the function is well defined and f(3) = 9.
steps: Both agree, so f is well defined at 3
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the two values

quiz.q: Why is g(x) = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 and 3x for 2 ≤ x ≤ 10 NOT a function?
options: At x = 2 the rules give 4 and 6, two different images
quiz.explain: A function must give exactly one image. At the shared point x = 2 the pieces disagree.
steps: One input with two images breaks the rule of a function
Not a function: at x = 2 the rules give 4 and 6
Answer: At x = 2 the rules give 4 and 6, two different images
quiz.mistake: Thinks having two formulas is the problem

quiz.q: If f(x) = 3x − 5 and g(x) = x², what is (2f + g)(1)?
quiz.explain: 2f(1) = 2(−2) = −4 and g(1) = 1, so the sum is −3.
quiz.mistake: Doubles g as well, or adds before doubling

teach.ask: Gappu wants to divide one function by another. Explain how to add, multiply and divide real functions and how to get the domain.
teach.praise: Combine the values, keep the common domain, and never divide by zero. Easy peasy!
teach.nudge: When you form f/g, which extra points must you throw out of the domain?

revise.summary: Real functions can be added, subtracted, multiplied and divided point by point on their common domain, and for f/g we also remove points where g(x) = 0. Piecewise rules must agree where they overlap.
focus: Compute (f ± g)(a), (fg)(a), (αf)(a) and (f/g)(a)
Find the domain of f/g by removing zeros of g
Check whether a piecewise rule is a well-defined function
Find a linear function from two values
remember: (f ± g)(x) = f(x) ± g(x) and (fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g
(f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g, excluding g(x) = 0
(αf)(x) = α f(x)
traps: Don't forget to remove the zeros of g from the domain of f/g
Overlapping pieces of a piecewise rule must give the same value, or it is not a function
